connections.feedback: Yes. The Constitution is the highest law in the country. Every other law must follow it.
Not this one. The Declaration of Independence said the colonies were free from Britain. It is not the highest law.
Close, but no. The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments. They are a part of the Constitution.
No. The Articles of Confederation were the first plan of government. The Constitution replaced them.

connections.feedback: Correct. The Constitution is the supreme law of the land. Laws made by Congress, states and courts must agree with it.
The Declaration of Independence explains why the colonies separated from Britain. It is a founding document, but it does not set the rules of government.
Laws passed by Congress are important, but they must follow the Constitution. If a law conflicts with it, courts can strike the law down.
The Articles of Confederation were the first national plan of government. They were replaced by the Constitution.

connections.feedback: Yes. The legislative branch (Congress) makes laws.
Yes. The executive branch, led by the President, carries out and enforces laws.
Yes. The judicial branch, the courts, explains the laws and decides disputes about them.
The armed forces are important, but they are part of the executive branch. The military is not a separate branch of the national government.

connections.feedback: Yes. Congress writes and passes the laws of the country.
Not quite. The President signs laws or says no to them. The President does not write them.
No. The Supreme Court decides what laws mean. It does not pass laws.
No. The Cabinet is a group of leaders who advise the President. They do not pass laws.

connections.feedback: Correct. The Constitution makes the President the commander in chief. This keeps the military under the control of an elected civilian leader.
Congress has important war powers: it declares war and pays for the military. But it does not command the forces. That role belongs to the President.
The Supreme Court is the top court. It decides legal cases and does not command the armed forces.
Cabinet members lead departments and advise the President. The President, not the Cabinet, is the commander in chief.

connections.feedback: Yes. Freedom of speech is in the First Amendment.
Yes. The First Amendment protects the freedom to practice any religion or none.
Yes. Freedom of the press means the government cannot generally control what news outlets publish.
This right is in the Second Amendment, not the First. The First Amendment covers religion, speech, press, assembly and petition.

connections.feedback: Correct. The Thirteenth Amendment, approved after the Civil War, ended slavery in the United States.
The Fifteenth Amendment says a citizen's right to vote cannot be denied because of race. It came after slavery had already ended.
The Nineteenth Amendment gave women the right to vote. It came much later, in the twentieth century.
The First Amendment protects freedoms such as speech and religion. It does not deal with slavery.

connections.feedback: Correct. Ratified after the Civil War, the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery. Learners often mix it up with the next two amendments, so teach the three together.

The Fourteenth Amendment addressed citizenship and equal protection. It built on the Thirteenth but did not itself end slavery. A useful teaching point: separate ending slavery from defining citizenship.
The Fifteenth Amendment protects the vote from denial on grounds of race. It is the third of the three post-war amendments.
The Twenty-Sixth Amendment lowered the voting age to eighteen. It is unrelated to slavery.

connections.feedback: Correct. The Fourteenth Amendment defines citizenship by birth in the country and guarantees equal protection and due process against the states.
The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery. The question asks about citizenship and equal protection, which the Fourteenth Amendment covers.
The Fifteenth Amendment protects voting from racial denial. It does not define citizenship or state the equal protection principle.
The First Amendment protects freedoms such as speech and religion. Equal protection language is in the Fourteenth.

connections.feedback: Yes. In a representative democracy, citizens elect representatives who make decisions for them.
Also defensible. Many people call the United States a republic, a government with elected leaders and a constitution. The two terms overlap, so either may be taught.
connections.notes: Republic and representative democracy are used for the same system in many classrooms. Some tutors reserve 'republic' for emphasis on constitutional limits. Accepting both avoids penalising a correct use.

connections.feedback: A monarchy is ruled by a king or queen, usually by inheritance. Citizens do not elect the ruler.
In a direct democracy people vote on laws themselves. The national government of the United States does not work this way.
